newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-NICKLAUSES MAKE IT A FATHER-AND-SON OPEN.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-NICKLAUSES MAKE IT A FATHER-AND-SON OPEN.

text.p: One of Jack Nicklaus's very few unfulfilled wishes in golf will come true on Thursday when he plays in the same U.S. Open as one of his sons.

"I always wanted to be able to play in a U.S. Open with one of my sons," Nicklaus said Wednesday after a practice round with son Gary as they prepared for Thursday's first round. "I am really appreciative of the USGA giving me the opportunity."

The elder Nicklaus, who will be competing in a record 41st consecutive Open and his 150th major championship, was granted a special exemption for this Open, while Gary, 28, made it into the 156-man field through qualifying tournaments.

While the two Nicklauses will not be playing together in the first two rounds of the Open, their participation marks only the fourth time in history that father and son have played in the same U.S. Open.
The last time a father-son duo played in the same Open was in 1982, when Gary and Wayne Player teed it up at Pebble Beach.

Nicklaus, who at age 57 is the oldest player here, said that he had wished his other three sons, Jackie, Steven and Michael, could have played in an Open with him, but only Gary so far has qualified for the championship.
The journey was not always easy for Gary, according to his father, who also has one daughter, Nancy Jean.
"The first time Gary tried to qualify for the Open, I caddied for him," Jack related. "After he parred the first two holes, he asked for a 4-iron on his next approach.
"I looked in the bag and said, 'Do you want your 4-iron or mine.'" The bag had one too many clubs and Gary was penalised two strokes for each hole he had played.
"A 4-shot penalty -- thanks to his caddie," Nicklaus said sheepishly, still obviously embarrassed by his faux pas.
Gary, who has played on several small tours recently without much success, said he was delighted to be playing in the Open with his father, who has won an unsurpassed four Opens.
"That's a little extra special -- very special -- playing with my dad," he said.
Gary, the second youngest son, admitted that it had not always been easy to be the son of one of the most famous people in sports, but he had no complaints.
"It's a tough name to carry. Those are big footprints to fill," he acknowledged, "But over the years I've learned to cope with it."
The son offered one anecdote about growing up in the Nicklaus family. Jack and his wife, Barbara, would always attend their childrens' sports events.
"Before I played," Gary said, "I would wonder how many people would be coming out to watch my dad watch me play."
Jack was asked if he would try to watch his son play on Thursday, when Gary plays about four hours ahead of his father.
"I might go out and see some of it," Jack said. "But I've got a golf tournament to play -- and I have trouble enough walking this course once."
Then Nicklaus thought for a minute. "I guess Mom's the one who's going to go 36 (holes) tomorrow."
Nicklaus also admitted that the presence of his son in the field -- and his desire to see him win -- would somewhat change his thinking about this championship.
"I always wanted to win every tournament I entered," Nicklaus said. "This is the only tournament I've ever entered where I'd like to finish second."
